content.p: Gerald Francis Ridsdale, a Catholic priest from Ballarat in western Victoria, pleaded guilty again and again over three decades to sexually abusing children. Australian media called him the country's most prolific paedophile priest. His convictions covered more than 70 children, and his sentence was extended repeatedly as new victims came forward. He was laicised after his first convictions in 1993 and had been in prison since 1994 when he died there on Tuesday 18 February 2025, aged 90.

His case matters beyond his own crimes. The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse used it to show how a diocese moved a known offender from parish to parish, and a civil settlement in 2019 followed the Church's admission in court documents that it knew of a complaint against him from 1975.

According to a timeline in The Courier, Ridsdale studied for the priesthood at Corpus Christi College in Werribee from 1954 to 1958, and the paper says his offending began there. He was ordained at St Patrick's Cathedral in Ballarat on 25 July 1961. Moody Law, a firm that has acted for survivors, counts 16 appointments in his 29 years as a priest, an average of 1.8 years each.

The Courier's timeline shows how short his stays were. He filled in at five parishes in his first years, including Horsham, Inglewood, Camperdown and Ballarat North. He was parish priest at Warrnambool from 1970 to 1971, Apollo Bay in 1974 and 1975, and Edenhope from April 1976 to July 1977, according to Moody Law. In 1980 he went on study leave to the National Pastoral Institute and, the paper says, offended there. From 1982 to 1985 he worked at the Catholic Enquiry Centre in Sydney, where the centre's director said at the end of 1983 that he wanted him out. In 1986 he held short posts in the Sydney archdiocese before returning to Horsham, where a written complaint about his offending was made in August 1987.

The Courier reported that he abused children, mainly boys and many of them altar boys, in the sacristy, the presbytery and the confessional, in his car, and around Mass, first communions, confirmations and weddings. It also described him leading a funeral and then taking two of the dead man's children away to abuse them. He set up a drop-in centre in Inglewood in 1975, and in 1994 he admitted to an insurance investigator that it was a trap.

Ridsdale described his own method to the Royal Commission. "It's obvious now to me that a pattern would have been, or a way of seeking victims, would have been to look for the vulnerable or to recognise the vulnerable," he said. "I would have made sure that I was in a situation where there was no one else around and I would have told the children to keep quiet about it." He said of his time in Mortlake in the early 1980s: "I got out of control again. I went haywire there." Broken Rites spokesman Wayne Chamley told The Courier that in Mortlake it was considered he had abused every child in the primary school, and that parishioners later removed the building where he abused children, row by row.

According to The Courier's account of the Royal Commission hearings, two Ballarat bishops were aware of his offending, one from his first year in the priesthood, and two Sydney archbishops were aware of "sexual problems" and that he should be kept from children. The sources disagree on the year of that first complaint. The ABC reported Ridsdale telling an insurance investigator that Bishop James O'Collins knew of a complaint in 1962, while The Courier's timeline places a complaint from a boarding-school boy in his first year, 1961. A defence the Ballarat Diocese filed, reported by the ABC in 2017, said that O'Collins was never aware of the offending.

The Guardian's obituary summarised the commission's findings: the diocese had been aware of Ridsdale's offending from the 1960s, and there was no question that Bishop Ronald Mulkearns knew by 1982. The commission found it "implausible" that Mulkearns did not tell a meeting of consultors about the complaints when they discussed moving Ridsdale from Mortlake to Sydney. George Pell, later a cardinal, had lived with Ridsdale in the 1970s and walked with him to court in 1993. The commission found Pell had thought, as early as 1973, about the prudence of Ridsdale taking boys on overnight camps. Pell said he had been deceived about the reasons for the Mortlake move, and the commission rejected that. Fox News reported that Pell denied any previous knowledge of criminal allegations against Ridsdale.

Ridsdale himself told the commission that the church should have notified the authorities. "I'd say definitely," he said. He said he was sorry that the bishop he first discussed his offending with had not gone to the police.

The first case began in May 1993, when he admitted indecently assaulting eight children, according to The Courier, and served three months in jail. He has been in prison since 1994. Further sentences followed.

In April 2014 Judge Michael Rozenes sentenced him to eight years with a five-year minimum for abusing 14 children, some as young as four, offences that came to light after the Victorian parliamentary inquiry into child sex abuse. "You used your position within the Church to facilitate your offending, befriending the complainants under the guise of the 'friendly priest'," the judge said.

On 13 April 2017 he pleaded guilty by video link to 20 offences against 10 boys and a girl, including rape, attempted rape and buggery, committed between 1961 and 1988 at places including Merbein, Edenhope, Riverside, Mortlake and Quantong. In August 2017 he admitted 23 charges, among them two of rape and one of buggery, concerning 12 children aged 6 to 13. The prosecutor described one girl whose father brought her to the priest, and a nine-year-old altar boy who was told "God will forgive all of your sins" while he was being raped. A survivor's statement said, "I feel like a piece of meat handed around for anyone to take a bite of."

On 31 August 2017 Judge Irene Lawson sentenced him, describing "unprecedented and grave offending over 30 years". "Throughout the period from 1961 to 1988 whilst an ordained priest you committed sexual offences against 65 children on a more or less continuous basis," she said. The ABC reported the new term as at least three more years, making a total of 33 years in prison; the ABC said he would be eligible for parole in 2022. The judge said it was "increasingly likely" he would die in jail.

The figures reported for his total sentence vary with the date and outlet. The Courier gave an effective total of 28 years in one passage and 36 in another; the ABC called it 29 years in 2019; Fox News said 39 years in 2023; and The Guardian said a maximum of 40 years in 2025. These probably reflect each new extension, but the pages do not reconcile them.

By 2023 Ridsdale was 89 and, according to Fox News, unable to walk since mid-2022. He pleaded guilty by video link from a prison hospital to indecently assaulting a 13-year-old boy in 1987 at Horsham, which was reported as a 72nd victim and a 193rd conviction. Fox News said his earliest release date had by then been extended to April 2027, after he admitted abusing two brothers in 1981 and 1982. The Guardian reported that he admitted another eight charges in the August before his death, and that at the last hearing he attended he said only "I'm guilty". It also reported that he had been bedridden since a fall in November 2022, in chronic pain with muscle wasting.

When he died, advocacy groups said his death did not erase the harm to survivors. Bravehearts chief executive Alison Geale said it "does not erase the immense suffering he inflicted on innocent children and their families."

The ABC reported in 2015 that in 1971 all the male teachers and the chaplain at St Alipius primary school in Ballarat were molesting children, and survivors said the region's suicide rate was "through the roof" because of that legacy. That is campaigner Peter Blenkiron's claim; the page gives no statistics.

Civil claims met resistance. In 2017 a lawyer for a man abused by Ridsdale in 1980 said the Ballarat Diocese was denying circumstances that the County Court had already accepted at sentencing. Bishop Paul Bird, named as defendant in place of the dead bishops, said the diocese would cooperate if the matter could not be settled through alternative dispute resolution. The ABC described the "Ellis defence", under which the Church argued it did not legally exist as an entity that could be sued. The Royal Commission recommended scrapping it, and Victoria's parliament closed the loophole by legislation in 2018.

In September 2019 a man known as JCB, raped by Ridsdale in Mortlake in 1982 at the age of nine, reached a settlement with the Church in the Victorian Supreme Court. The ABC said it was expected to exceed $1 million, and that in court documents the Church conceded awareness of a complaint about Ridsdale from 1975. His lawyer Judy Courtin called it a "landmark" that could open the door for hundreds of other claims.
